justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for gold prices across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, I anchored near recent trading levels around $1,935, assuming no major macro surprises and relatively thin overnight news flow. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects gold's tendency to benefit from lingering uncertainty around Federal Reserve policy, dollar softness, and geopolitical tensions that were present in the background at the time of the forecast. The one-month estimate of roughly $1,975 embeds a mild continuation of those tailwinds without assuming any dramatic catalyst.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which reflects fundamental differences in forecasting difficulty. At one day, gold is relatively anchored by technical trading ranges and intraday liquidity, so the 90% interval spans roughly $114. By one week, scheduled events like Fed speakers, CPI prints, or geopolitical developments can meaningfully shift sentiment, widening the interval to about $240. At one month, the range opens to $550, reflecting the compounding uncertainty of multiple economic data releases, central bank decisions, and shifts in real yields or the dollar index, all of which have historically been strong drivers of gold prices.

Specific risks on the upside that could push gold well above my stated intervals include an unexpected escalation in geopolitical conflict, a sudden financial stress event driving safe-haven flows, or a sharp dovish pivot from the Fed signaling earlier rate cuts. On the downside, a surprisingly strong U.S. jobs report or inflation print could reinforce a higher-for-longer rate narrative, strengthening the dollar and pushing real yields higher, which would be historically bearish for gold. A rapid de-escalation of geopolitical tensions could also reduce the risk premium embedded in current prices.

It is worth noting that gold markets can also be influenced by large institutional positioning shifts or sovereign central bank buying programs, which are difficult to forecast and can move prices in ways that are largely disconnected from macro fundamentals over short windows. These idiosyncratic flows represent a genuine tail risk in either direction and are one reason I chose a relatively wide one-month interval despite the seemingly modest point estimate drift.
